case_studies.title: SARA: SLO-Aware Resource Allocation for Disaggregated Agentic LLM Services
case_studies.abstract: Recent advances in large language models (LLMs) are driving the emergence of multi-modal and agentic services for mobile users through cloud and edge infrastructures, where long-context workloads pose daunting challenges for inference latency. Existing disaggregated LLM serving systems largely rely on hardware profiling, configuration enumeration, or heuristic scheduling, offering limited analytical guidance for cost-efficient resource allocation. In this paper, we propose SARA, a Service level objectives (SLOs)-Aware Resource Allocation framework for disaggregated agentic LLM serving systems,
case_studies.summary: SARA tackles the challenge of efficiently allocating cloud resources for long‑context LLM inference by using service‑level objectives (SLOs) to guide the distribution of compute across disaggregated systems. The authors built a framework that automatically adjusts resource allocation based on real‑time SLO monitoring, and they demonstrated a measurable reduction in cost while meeting latency targets.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure for LLM services, here is what to do: 1) deploy SARA to collect SLO metrics and current resource utilisation, 2) use its optimisation module to redistribute GPU/CPU time across your disaggregated nodes, 3) monitor the resulting latency and cost impact to validate the model’s effectiveness.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper introduces a novel SLO-aware resource allocation framework (SARA) for disaggregated agentic LLM services, which is a fresh concept for IT engineers dealing with cloud and edge LLM deployments. It offers actionable insights into cost‑efficient scheduling and latency optimisation, directly relevant to infrastructure, MLOps, and cloud cost management. However, the practical deployment details are limited, and the immediate applicability within 90 days is moderate (e.g., could guide tuning of existing LLM serving stacks but requires integration effort).

case_studies.title: Flash-dLLM: IO-Aware KV Caching and Parallel Decoding for Fast, Memory-Efficient Diffusion LLMs
case_studies.abstract: Diffusion Large Language Models (dLLMs) have recently emerged as a promising alternative to autoregressive LLMs by enabling non-autoregressive text generation. However, their practical deployment remains limited by inefficient inference, largely due to the absence of effective Key-Value (KV) caching and scalable parallel decoding mechanisms. Existing acceleration methods typically study KV caching and parallel decoding in isolation, overlooking the I/O bottlenecks that arise when cache reuse and parallel token verification are jointly applied. In this work, we introduce $\textbf{Flash-dLLM}$,
case_studies.summary: Flash‑dLLM tackles slow, memory‑hungry inference in diffusion‑based LLMs by adding I/O‑aware KV caching and parallel decoding, achieving up to 2‑3× faster token generation while cutting memory usage.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage inference workloads for diffusion LLMs, implement Flash‑dLLM’s I/O‑aware KV cache to reduce disk/SSD traffic and enable their parallel decoding engine to cut GPU utilisation, then monitor latency and cost savings.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel, IO‑aware KV caching and parallel decoding scheme for diffusion LLMs, which could improve inference speed and memory usage for on‑prem or cloud deployments. For an IT engineer, this could inform choices around GPU/CPU allocation and model hosting strategies, especially when considering cost and latency trade‑offs. The applicability is moderate: it requires an environment where diffusion LLMs are deployed, and the benefits are most visible to engineers managing inference infrastructure. Thus the novelty is moderate (20/33), the IT relevance is high (25/33) due to potential impact on cloud and on‑prem inference workloads, and the 90‑day value is low (10/34) because the techniques are research‑level and would need integration work before deployment.

case_studies.title: Grow the Harness, Not the Context: From Strategy-Free Scaffolds to Reusable Specialist Agents
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents often handle streams of related tasks, yet standard harnesses repeatedly ask the model to reconstruct the same control decisions inside each task's context. We study whether task feedback can instead turn recurring control into reusable executable code, while reserving LLM calls for task-specific semantic reasoning. We introduce Growing Harness, a failure-guided training paradigm that learns the agent harness itself from a strategy-free scaffold that exposes fixed model and tool interfaces but encodes no task-solving controller. Overall, the contribution is both novel and relevant, with a clear, near‑term implementation path.

case_studies.title: Toolcompass: Guiding Tool Trialing, Not Suppressing It
case_studies.abstract: Large language model (LLM) agents must generalize from tools seen during training to unseen tools at deployment. A key challenge is tool trialing, i.e., excessive trials waste the interaction budget, whereas selective trials enable exploration of unfamiliar tools. Existing outcome-based post-training leaves wasteful trials unguided, while turn-level supervision may suppress necessary exploration. We introduce ToolCompass, a post-training framework that guides tool trialing by organizing tool-call representations according to shared functions. case_studies.summary: ToolCompass helps large‑language‑model agents decide when to try new tools, reducing wasted trials while still exploring unfamiliar tools. It builds a post‑training framework that groups tool calls by function and guides agents to choose trials that are likely useful. The result is fewer unnecessary calls and better use of interaction budgets. This is relevant for any organisation deploying LLM‑powered tools.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud infrastructure that uses LLM agents to trigger scripts or services, here is what to do: 1) integrate ToolCompass into your agent pipeline to map tool calls by function; 2) configure the guidance thresholds to match your interaction budget; 3) monitor trial counts and adjust to keep trials focused on high‑value functions.

It offers a novel insight into reducing trial costs and improving exploration, but it lacks a concrete, ready‑to‑implement solution or a clear integration path for existing SaaS or cloud tools.
